result:
There is a particular kind of hope in a half-used notebook.

Not a new notebook. New notebooks are tyrants. Their pages are so clean that every sentence feels like a decision about who you intend to become. You buy one imagining orderly thoughts, perhaps a better handwriting, perhaps a life in which you remember what you went into the kitchen to do.

Then, on page one: a grocery list.

On page two: an idea you can no longer decipher.

On page three: a telephone number with no name, which gradually acquires the menace of a clue in a detective story.

And then, somewhere around page seventeen, the notebook becomes useful.

You have spoiled its perfection. Now you can write.

A half-used notebook has learned to accommodate you. It contains proof that you are capable of beginning things and equally capable of forgetting them. There is a diagram of a bookshelf you never built. A sentence overheard on a bus: *He was a very punctual liar.* Three attempts to calculate the cost of something you eventually bought without calculating.

Between these entries, there is still room.

I like objects that leave room. A kitchen table with scratches. A city with a vacant lot where wildflowers have taken over. A recipe that says “until it looks right,” trusting you with a judgment no timer can make.

A notebook can hold a serious thought beside a reminder to buy dish soap. Neither entry needs to apologize for being there. The dish soap gets bought; the thought waits a few weeks, then finds its way into a letter.

Perhaps that is what makes the half-used notebook hopeful. You open it looking for the number of a plumber and find an idea worth another try.

You turn to the next available page. There’s a faint ring from a coffee cup near the bottom, but plenty of space above it.
